analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacies and wholesalers import FDA-approved prescription drugs sold more cheaply abroad.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to let prescription drugs be imported from countries where they sell for less sat in a House committee for 20 months, never got a vote, and died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Americans pay more than people in other countries for the same FDA-approved medicines. This bill would require drug makers to keep shipping and labeling records for drugs they sell abroad, and to share those records with U.S. importers, so pharmacies and wholesalers could bring those same approved drugs back into the country and compete on price. It was introduced in May 1999 with 95 cosponsors from both parties, sent to the House Commerce Committee, and never brought up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: American patients and anyone paying out of pocket for prescription drugs, especially seniors and the uninsured, because imported versions of the same FDA-approved drugs would create price competition and a legal route to lower prices.

how_it_helps.text: The bill opens a legal channel for importing FDA-approved prescription drugs that were exported or made in registered foreign plants, letting U.S. importers buy them at the lower prices charged abroad.

Drug manufacturers must maintain records for each shipment showing it meets manufacturing and labeling standards, and must provide those records to qualified U.S. importers on request, which is what makes safe importation verifiable.
The bill covers prescription drugs and insulin, the categories that drive out-of-pocket costs for chronic conditions.

It directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to write criteria governing the records and labeling so imported drugs can be shown to be domestically approved and compliant, and to limit the fees manufacturers can charge for providing records.
Supporters spanning both parties — 76 Democrats, 18 Republicans, and one Independent — signed on, which suggests broad congressional appetite for lowering drug prices.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose some control over the U.S. market and face pressure to narrow the price gap between the U.S. and other countries; they also bear the cost of keeping and sharing shipment records.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is safety: imported drugs travel through foreign supply chains, and critics argue that even with record requirements, regulators cannot fully verify that pills arriving at a U.S. counter match what was approved. The bill tries to address this by requiring compliance records for every shipment, but the risk is not zero.

Savings are not guaranteed: manufacturers could limit export volumes or the bill's effectiveness depends on regulations the HHS Secretary must write, and if manufacturers raised foreign prices to close the U.S. gap, patients would see little relief.
The recordkeeping mandate applies to every shipment, not just ones destined for importation, which is an administrative cost imposed on manufacturers across their export business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a legal path to the lower prices Americans already see charged abroad for identical FDA-approved drugs — is large for the tens of millions who pay U.S. prices. The safety concerns are real but were addressed head-on by the bill's compliance-record requirements, and the main cost falls on brand-name drug makers' pricing power rather than on patients. The bill was a reasonably designed version of a policy idea, and its failure was not a failure of design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and its health subcommittee in May 1999, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Marion Berry (D-AR) introduced the bill on May 20, 1999, with original cosponsors including Bernie Sanders (I), Jo Ann Emerson (R), Dana Rohrabacher (R), Neil Abercrombie (D), and John Lewis (D).
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce, and on June 15, 1999, to that committee's Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
Over the following twenty months, the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — only sponsor introductory remarks in April 2000.
By the end of the Congress the bill had 95 cosponsors from both parties, but it never reached a vote in the full House or Senate and expired on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who kept their protected U.S. market and the price gap with other countries; American patients kept paying U.S. prices for drugs sold cheaper abroad.

for.name: Rep. Marion Berry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the record in April 2000.

for.name: 95 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad bipartisan support.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in May 1999 and, in twenty months, held no hearing or markup and never reported it to the floor.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers' lobbying campaign
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained campaign against reimportation legislation, arguing imported drugs could not be guaranteed safe.

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list was bipartisan — 76 Democrats, 18 Republicans, and 1 Independent out of 95 — and the original introduction itself paired a Democrat with two Republicans and an Independent; the obstacle was not a floor vote but the committee never acting.

industries.note: Reimportation would let cheaper versions of their own FDA-approved drugs come back into the U.S. market, eroding the price premium American patients pay. Their interest in blocking import laws runs directly against consumers who pay those prices.

industries.industry: U.S. pharmacies, wholesalers, and drug importers
industries.note: The bill creates a legal importation channel and requires manufacturers to hand over shipment records to qualified importers, giving these businesses a new lower-cost supply source they can pass on to customers.
